case_name: Kashiram v State of Madhya Pradesh
respondent:
State of Madhya Pradesh
Supreme Court of India

16 October 1998
Criminal Appeal No. 57 of 1997
The Judgment was delivered by : M. Srinivasan, J.
1.  The appellant and six other persons stood prosecuted for offences under Ss. 147, 148, 302 read with 149 and 307/149. They were acquitted by the Additional District Judge, Narisinghgarh, Distt. Rajgarh (Byara), W.P. State. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the acquittal of five persons but reversed the Judgment of the trial Judge with reference to the appellant and another by name Ram Singh. The appellant was convicted for offences under Ss. 302 and 324 IPC and sentenced to imprisonment for life u/s 302 and imprisonment for four months and a fine of Rs. 1000/- u/s 324. We are not concerned with the other accused as he has not come to this Court.
The case of the prosecution is shortly as follows :
2. There was prior enmity between the accused persons on the one side and Gorelal
facts: There was prior enmity between the accused persons on the one side and Gorelal and others on the other.
The accused persons formed an unlawful assembly and on 29.12.86 at about 2 P.M. committed the murder of Gorelal in the jungle of Padiliya Khadi.
Ram Singh and the appellant shot the deceased with a gun.
They caused gunshot injuries to Nankram, Deochand, Beni Singh and Ramesh in the attempt to murder them.
Sewa Ram (PW1) was working in his field when he saw a bullock cart coming from forest side.
On hearing sounds of screaming and wailing, he went to the cart and found the dead body of Gorelal.

He was informed by Hiralal s/o Ramratan that the appellant, his brother Bhanwaria, Amritlal, Daryhao Singh, Kailash, Ram Singh and Pappu Killed Gorelal in Chhapra and that Ram Singh and the appellant fired guns at Gorelal.
Thereafter Sevaram went to the police Station at Kotra and reported the matter at 5.50 P.M., the same day.
J.S. Tomar (PM9), SHO registered offences u/ss 147, 148, 302, 307 read with 149 vide Crime No. 148/86.
petitioner_arguments: The FIR was not lodged on the same day but it was done only on the next day.
The appellant has proved alibi and he was not at the place of occurrence.
No doctor has been examined to prove the alleged injuries of eye witnesses.
Nor have they produced any medical certificate.
The evidence of the prosecution witnesses is full of discrepancies.
The driver of the tractor recovered by the prosecution was not examined by it, and he has been examined by the defence.
His evidence corroborated by the damage on the tractor proves conclusively the defence version.
The Judgment of the High Court is perfunctory and unsustainable.
respondent_arguments: All the witnesses of the prosecution are consistent in stating that the appellant fired the gun after getting it from Ram Singh.
The appellant has failed to plead or prove alibi and DW1 was not the driver of the tractor in question.
No suggestion of alibi was put to the prosection witnesses by the defence counsel.
The judgment of the high Court does not warrant any interference.
court_reasoning: All the five witnesses have categorically spoken to the presence of the appellant on the spot and his firing the gun after taking it from Ram Singh.
The argument that no doctor has been examined to prove the injuries of the witnesses is without any substance.
Nothing has been elicited in the cross-examination to enable the court to discard their version of having suffered injuries.
On the other hand, suggestions have been made in the cross examination as if there was a fight between the two groups at the spot.
The main plank of the argument of the appellant's counsel was 'alibi'.
There are several circumstances which disprove the case of alibi.
There was no consistency in the suggestions made to prosecution witnesses when they were cross-examined.
A suggestion was made to PW2 that he himself and the members of his group attacked the appellant and his driver.
The evidence of DW1 who claims to be the driver of the tractor which was found on the scene of occurrence.
But the number of the tractor given by him is different from the number of the tractor seized.
His entire evidence is wholly unreliable.
The High Court has rightly characterised him as got-up witness and his evidence is rejected.
In the facts and circumstances of the case, there is no difficulty in rejecting the version of the appellant that he was not present on the scene of occurrence at the relevant time.

The other matters relied on by the learned counsel for the appellant in support of his contention that the evidence of the prosecution witnesses is unacceptable are not of much significance or sufficient importance to negative the reliability of the prosecution witnesses.
holding: The appeal fails and is dismissed.
The sentences awarded by the High Court are quite appropriate and do not find any warrant to interfere with the same.
